prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, explaining how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade and linking trade models to firm-level data.

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI changed the unit of analysis in trade from industries to firms. They created a framework that fits exporter premia, selection and reallocation in firm-level microdata. It added a new channel for the gains from trade, and it has been used for more than twenty years in macro, IO, development and policy evaluation. Krugman's 2008 prize covered scale economies and trade patterns, and this is a distinct discovery with stronger empirical discipline. The attribution is comparatively clean for a two-name set: Melitz is the core model and Helpman is the central architect of the wider heterogeneous-firm agenda. After reading colleagues' openings I keep B038 first. My reasons are its conceptual break, its empirical grounding, and the fact that the credit problem is smaller here than in the New Keynesian case. Counts of support are not part of this reasoning.
statement.case_against: Credit is not fully captured by the ballot. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on closely related firm-level trade work, and Redding's later quantitative contributions are real. A Melitz-Helpman prize could be read as under-crediting that literature. The gains-from-trade magnitudes also depend on elasticity and functional-form assumptions. Helpman's separate appearance on B030 means his credit has to be accounted for once.

responses.point: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint credit cycle. The financial-accelerator line of Gertler and Gilchrist is partly covered by the 2022 prize to Bernanke, so a two-name award is the cleanest.
responses.response: I accept this and revise my opening view. I had proposed Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. The accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke-Gertler and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist, and Bernanke is already a laureate. Adding Gertler therefore blurs the discovery and also blurs his position across B015 and B050. A Kiyotaki-Moore award is better defined. I still rank B038 slightly higher, because the empirical identification of the original collateral-amplification mechanism is more mixed than its theoretical influence, as you note. I would keep B050 as the first alternative.

responses.point: The New Keynesian framework is the strongest case on influence and maturity. Calvo and Taylor supply staggered pricing and contracts, and Woodford gives the micro-founded synthesis. Omitting Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific weight and the maturity. My difficulty is attribution. Eight credited names for three places means any trio is contestable. My own trio (Woodford, Gali, Gertler) and your trio (Woodford, Taylor, Calvo) rest on different readings of what the discovery is. Yours credits the originating building blocks. Mine credits the canonical model and its policy analysis. The choice is a judgement call rather than something the evidence settles, so I would not use B015's breadth of influence to settle it. I also place the post-2021 Phillips-curve debate among the open issues. It does not displace the framework, but it makes the definition of the discovery less sharp than for B038. I keep B015 as an alternative and not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Melitz's model is field-defining, and Helpman is the natural co-recognition. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have strong claims outside the credited names, so a narrow laureate set could be contested. The 2008 trade prize is also a possible overlap.
responses.response: I share your reading of the core contribution and of the Krugman overlap. Krugman's prize concerned trade patterns and location under increasing returns. Melitz is about selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms, tested on firm-level data. I do not fully resolve the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum concern. The credited list limits the permitted laureates, and the citation should therefore describe the specific discovery, the firm-selection model and its welfare implications, and not the whole firm-level trade literature. That wording makes the narrower set defensible without implying that others' contributions are lesser.

responses.point: Helpman may be seen as better credited under a broader trade-theory recognition, and Redding is a plausible alternative third name.
responses.response: Redding's contributions to quantitative and spatial trade are important. They extend and apply the heterogeneous-firm framework, and they are a later stage of the field. Adding him widens the citation toward quantitative trade and weakens the focus on a single discovery. I would keep the two-name set. Helpman's central role in the heterogeneous-firm agenda is hard to dispute, and it is separable from his trade-politics work on B030, so the credit is not double-counted by this citation.

responses.point: B036 deserves first place. The task framework and the trade-shock evidence combine a conceptual framework with credible identification and have very large influence.
responses.response: I agree on the influence and the quality of the evidence, which is why I place B036 in my top five. My reservations are about construction. The task and skill-premium strand and the China-shock strand have different authorship. The task framework overlaps with Acemoglu's 2024 recognition and Goldin's 2023 prize. The three-name set involves a hard choice among Katz, Dorn and Hanson. The China-shock magnitudes and persistence are still contested. B038 is better defined as a single discovery with a clean credit set.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to widen the credit to the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum literature or to Redding's quantitative extensions, and whether the three-person limit makes that feasible.
How sensitive the quantified gains from trade are to elasticity assumptions, and how much that weakens the empirical record.
How the committee would account for Helpman's candidacy on B030 alongside B038.
Whether the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore award or the diffuse New Keynesian credit is the better second candidate for the committee.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to the preferred part is apparent from the supplied profile. Melitz, Helpman and Redding are not listed among my co-authors. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (B016) and with Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud and Huiyu Li. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. They rank B015 first, so I have weighed their arguments as evidence only. B016 is not in my preferred configuration, and I have not adjudicated these ties.
